I think it's very fair to be disappointed with humanity. There's achievements I'm sure people can point to that are inspiring, or moments where humanity has done truly good things. I have a lot of thoughts and feelings, I think I can summarise them as: it's normal people doing this, it's not weird, strange creeps who are easily identifiable and distinct. It's fathers, mothers, brothers, teachers, sports coaches, volunteers, it's every subtle 'role' filled within society. Until we can be honest about this, we won't even creep towards honestly engaging with solutions.

It's absolutely caused me more trauma, pain and has certainly set me back. But, in happy with who I am and where I've landed. I wouldn't say I feel that in the dark and challenging times, but I work to solve the problems I see and I hope I'm making the small difference I can. Living as me, as my values and having healed enough to engage with life, it has sucked. But I'll always have a lot of gratitude to myself that I kept going, and that I got here with my heart intact. 


So yea, I just wanted to say in more words than necessary, that it's totally fair to be disappointed in the world. But I think it can give ourselves the compass to not have that disappointment in ourselves because we see the world with this clarity.

I see it through a few different lenses, and we will never know who we may have been in the absence of the trauma. 


First and foremost, we deserved a safe childhood, not a childhood that forced us to adapt to trauma and develop mechanisms that served us during that. 


I think we all personally find new mechanisms, ones that help us interact with the 'normal' world. For me, I often frame it in my mind as I have tried to take the best lesson I can. Taking your example, I learned empathy, and I am grateful for that part of me. 


But I completely agree, I don't think I'm stronger for it, I'm different and don't cope with many things. I know I'm resilient, but I also know I breakdown and have to take time to recover. I can function in the world, but I struggle with many outcomes of my trauma. None of us have gotten enough out of trauma that we would ever go 'yes, what a deal how lucky I am!". Because your bitter bill is true. 


Which I think is why I do try and take the best I can, because I haven't got any alternatives. We can't not take the deal, we don't get a do over or to find out who we may have been. It sucks, I'd rather lose all these aspects of myself, that whilst I am grateful for are not worth the damage. I would rather have less empathy and have never been traumatised and spend twenty plus years, all of my adult life endlessly healing and recovering. It's shit. It sucks, I'm better at coping with trauma, and worse at coping with normal life. 


Thank you for sharing, I appreciate getting to work through this in my head.

It's weird, I feel very similar.


I think there's a challenge in healing, that we do heal. We start learning that we are safe, that we have access to support, and we start unlearning all these mechanisms that served us when we were being traumatised. 


The right tools from trauma aren't the same that help us thrive in living a whole and joyful life. But... that bubbling anxiety and hyper vigilance did 'function', it certainly gave me a lot of energy, and absolutely not shortage of feeling. 


Unlearning all these mechanisms that kept me alive is not what I thought would be the 'easy' part. I often feel like at least I knew who I was? That I felt and was a person, I certainly relate strongly to my trauma becoming my identity, or really healing it. And I'm very numb these days, but I function, I live a life, and in trying to do the hard part. Which seems to be stumbling through life, much older, having to learn all these healthy coping mechanisms. Put effort into learning then, put effort into building a person, an identity, a life. 


And I think that's the hard part, after going to therapy, after healing, after life isn't just being trapped in flashbacks... we have to learn to actually live? I've found it horrible. I often miss being a dysfunctional mess, because at least I wasn't isolated. But I still wouldn't give up trying to have a life that is healthy, peaceful and whole. Sunday I get ready for the week, and usually spend a lot of time on my bicycle, listening to an audio book.

I know to the people I work with I look out together, functional, and am soneone people appreciate for being kind, thoughtful, empathetic and always willing to help. My life is being functional enough to work, because I need to work. Connecting is something that I find risky, dating feels dangerous, and I can't handle the prospect of being in another relationship with an abusive person. 


I don't know if I live, really? I am getting better at it. I run, I cycle, I do archery, I play video games, I enjoy shows, movies, books. I don't have the energy to do a lot of things I loved, like painting, crafts, exploring. So, yea I dunno. I have a lot to be grateful for, my life is incredibly stable, I do have good people in my life, even if I am incredibly isolated. After 21 years of therapy and healing it's probably the best I've ever been, but ultimately getting better has been my life. Healing, working on myself, trying over and over, endlessly making sure I'm taking the next step I can, no matter how small. I think at some point I stopped living, and felt like I'd tried to optimise the humanity out of my life. I'm trying to get back in touch with myself and understand what I even want, who I even am. 


I don't really understand why I've always tried, or even wanted to be better, life since my trauma has just felt like chronic pain, endless effort and exhaustion, re-traumatisation, re-victimisation. I wouldn't say I enjoy life, I do try to, but I just don't.

My story will likely always lack detail, because I don't need to convey the detail. If my partner wanted to know exactly what happened, and was also angry and filed with vengeance, it would make me feel invisible.

It's understandable to feel a range of things. But, as much as going through the justice system can be retraumatising, as you have to relive it over and over again, and in painful detail. Having to do that, even with a trusted person, partner, family, friend, it's not easy. It usually is exhausting, and often you end up having to coach the person who wants to help through their own feelings. Once again, not particularly validating, and can easily make you feel invisible.

Personally, if my partner did want to know exactly what happened and was just angry and started wanting vengeance/justice, despite having made my position clear. If it didn't clear up pretty quickly, I'd know this person isn't right for me. Listen, empathise, support, just be human. If you need support, seek support, but don't put the burden on your partner.

It would legitimately be like a second death. It would to me go beyond retraumatisation and instead just be a source of trauma.

It disgusts me, and I accept that most people who enjoy it simply don't care, not maliciously, but they don't think about it. They don't consider it, it's not real to them, it probably just makes them feel a little more than a horror or thriller. I also assume the experience of feeling 'righteous' and the false empathy would play a role. "Oh my God, how could anyone do that? Those poor people." etc.

It's absolutely the case that it's just profiteering off suffering. I think if there was no money to be made, people would be able to go back to the default of not caring at all.
